description_full: Texas Instruments Incorporated designs, manufactures, and sells semiconductors to electronics designers and manufacturers in the United States, China, the rest of Asia, Europe, the Middle East, Africa, Japan, and internationally. It operates through Analog and Embedded Processing segments. The Analog segment offers power products to manage power requirements across various voltage levels, including battery-management solutions, DC/DC switching regulators, AC/DC and isolated controllers and converters, power switches, linear regulators, voltage references, multiphase controllers and power stages, and lighting products. This segment also provides signal chain products that sense, condition, and measure real-world signals and convert them into data to be transferred or converted for further processing and control, such as amplifiers, data converters, interface products, motor drives, clocks, and logic and sensing products. The Embedded Processing segment offers microcontrollers, processors, wireless connectivity, and radar products; and applications processors for specific computing activity. It also provides DLP products primarily for use in projecting high-definition images; calculators; and application-specific integrated circuits. Its products are used in various markets, such as industrial, automotive, personal electronics, communications equipment, enterprise systems, calculators, and others. The company markets and sells its semiconductor products through direct sales and distributors, as well as through its website. Texas Instruments Incorporated was founded in 1930 and is headquartered in Dallas, Texas.

financial_summary: Texas Instruments Incorporated is a mega-cap technology business with a $253.6B market cap on $17.7B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -4% over the past three years and +3% annually across the full decade, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.
Returns on capital run at 38% against a 10% cost of capital — a 28-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat. Gross margins of 58% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $2.6B in free cash flow — roughly 15 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.43× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.2× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 11.1×.

Shareholder yield of 2.6% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sect: Its 34% operating margin runs 27pp above the Technology median (7%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
Its share of sector profits slightly exceeds its share of revenue (1.46x).
It accounts for 0.4% of sector revenue and 0.6% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-14.0% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 530 companies in the universe; the top four hold 29% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 87% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 17% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 44% and a beta of 1.11, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 1.74 vs 5y 1.14), so read it loosely.
Liquidity is deep, with about $1.5B traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 30% in the 2020 crash, 22% in the 2022 bear market and 57% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $125 (margin of safety -122%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models corroborate one another (dispersion 12%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $67.44 to $227 (P10-P90).
On multiples it looks expensive against Technology peers: P/E 36.0 vs 26.7, EV/EBITDA 24.2 vs 16.4 and P/FCF 97.4 vs 25.4 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 151% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 1.0% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 2.3% (vs the 8% bar).
The 29 covering analysts target $337 on average, 21% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 38% clears the cost of capital of 10.0% by 28pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.50).
It runs a 58% gross margin and converts 15% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.43x.
ROE of 31% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.1x equity multiplier).
It spends 11.8% of revenue on R&D and 2.4% on stock compensation (above the 2% gate).
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 1.2x net debt to EBITDA ($4.9B of cash against $14.0B of debt), with interest covered 11.1x.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 11.9, in the safe zone).
Working capital ties up about 235 days of sales, a drag on cash generation.
growth: Revenue has compounded at -4.1% over 3 years, 4.1% over 5 years and 3.1% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 13%).
At current returns, reinvesting 35% of profits supports about 13.3% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded -13.9% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Capex runs 2.4x depreciation (25.7% of sales), so it is building capacity for future growth.
Its Rule of 40 score is 16, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 9.6% on average.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.3%), and institutions hold 92%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (17 sales, net $31.9M sold).
It returns 2.6% a year to shareholders (0.6% in buybacks and 2.2% in dividends).
It has paid a dividend for 53 consecutive years, raising it 7.8% a year over the last five.
people: With about 33,000 employees, each generates about $536K of revenue, 1.4x the Technology median, and productivity has risen 3.4% a year.
That works out to $79K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $4.7M (9x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores poorly (8/10, lower is better).
